name: Sol
etymology_summary: From the Puerta del Sol, one of Madrid's medieval fortress gates during the 1520 Comuneros revolt. The gate may have had a sun carved on it, or faced east toward the sunrise.
source: Renfe Blog (renfe.com); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerta_del_Sol; Secretos de Madrid

name: Gran Via
etymology_summary: Named after the Gran Via boulevard ('Great Way'), Madrid's iconic avenue built 1910-1929 by demolishing hundreds of old buildings to create a grand east-west thoroughfare.

name: Tirso de Molina
etymology_summary: Named after Fray Gabriel Tellez (1579-1648), known by his pen name Tirso de Molina, a Mercedarian friar and playwright who created the character of Don Juan in 'El burlador de Sevilla'.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirso_de_Molina; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: La Latina
etymology_summary: Named after Beatriz Galindo 'La Latina' (1465-1534), a humanist and Latin scholar who served as tutor and advisor to Queen Isabel la Catolica.

name: Goya
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco de Goya (1746-1828), the great Spanish painter and printmaker. The street and plaza were named first; the station follows.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_de_Goya; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Arguelles
etymology_summary: Named after Agustin de Arguelles (1776-1844), a liberal lawyer and politician of the Cortes of Cadiz, known as 'El Divino' for his oratory.

name: Chueca
etymology_summary: Named after Federico Chueca (1846-1908), composer of the genero chico zarzuela, a form of Spanish light opera. His most famous work is 'La Gran Via'.

name: Embajadores
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de Embajadores. During the reign of Juan II of Castile (15th century), a plague outbreak forced foreign ambassadors from Tunis, Navarre, Aragon, and France to be quartered in country houses outside the city walls to avoid contagion. The area became the 'Campo de Embajadores' (Field of Ambassadors), and the street leading to it inherited the name. Appears on the Texeira map (1656).
source: Secretos de Madrid; Wikipedia; Texeira map 1656

name: Lavapies
etymology_summary: Disputed origin. (1) Topographical theory (favoured by Lorenzo Arribas, CVC 2008; Bazaco Palacios et al. 2013): rainwater rushing down the steep barranco (ravine) toward Glorieta de Embajadores literally washed pedestrians' feet in the unpaved streets. The 2013 paper 'Lavapies, barranco y arrabal' characterizes the area as a dramatic ravine, not merely a slope. (2) Jewish fountain legend: Jews washed feet before entering a nearby synagogue. Modern historians reject this: Urgorri's 1954 study of the 1453 census shows Jews lived dispersed across Madrid, not in a ghetto. (3) Posada/inn theory: travellers washed feet before sharing beds. (4) Moratin's underground springs theory (dismissed by Mesonero Romanos). Earliest document: 1441 land sale mentioning 'two agricultural plots at Lavapies' (Archivo de Villa). Medieval variants: 'Alavapies'/'Avapies' (1441-1498).
source: Lorenzo Arribas (CVC 2008: cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/noviembre_08/21112008_01.htm); Bazaco Palacios, Lorenzo Arribas & Real Gallego 2013 (academia.edu/4588123); Turra Historica 2021 (turrahistorica.com); Mesonero Romanos 'El antiguo Madrid' 1861; Madrid Archivo de Villa (earliest doc. 1441)

name: Chamberi
etymology_summary: Named after the neighbourhood, whose name derives from the French city of Chambery, capital of Savoy, though the transmission mechanism is debated. The most probable link is via Queen Barbara de Braganza, who founded the Royal Salesas Convent (c.1748) with nuns from Chambery/Annecy in Savoy; the toponym first appears on Chalmandrier's 1761 map. An alternative attributes it to Luisa Gabriela de Saboya (wife of Felipe V). The Napoleonic regiment theory is refuted by the 1761 map predating Napoleon. This station closed in 1966 and reopened as a museum ('Estacion Fantasma') in 2008.
source: Pedro de Repide; Chalmandrier map 1761; Chamberi30dias; Ayuntamiento de Madrid 'Historia de Chamberi'

name: Callao
etymology_summary: Named after the plaza, which commemorates the 1866 naval Battle of Callao against Peru.

name: Opera
etymology_summary: Named after the nearby Teatro Real (Royal Opera House), inaugurated in 1850.

name: Principe de Vergara
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Baldomero Espartero (1793-1879), military leader who was regent and prince of Vergara after the Convention of Vergara (1839).

name: Alfonso XIII
etymology_summary: Named after King Alfonso XIII (1886-1941), who inaugurated and helped fund the first Metro line in 1919.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_XIII; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Gregorio Maranon
etymology_summary: Named after Gregorio Maranon y Posadillo (1887-1960), physician, scientist, historian, and precursor of endocrinology in Spain.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorio_Mara%C3%B1%C3%B3n; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Paco de Lucia
etymology_summary: Named after Paco de Lucia (1947-2014), the legendary flamenco guitarist who revolutionized the genre and brought it international recognition.

name: Manuela Malasana
etymology_summary: Named after the nearby IES Manuela Malasana school, which is in turn named after Manuela Malasana Onoro (1791-1808), a young seamstress killed by French soldiers during the Dos de Mayo Uprising in Madrid. She was found carrying scissors which the French deemed a weapon, leading to her summary execution. She became a symbol of popular resistance against Napoleon.

name: Principe Pio
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco Pio de Saboya (1659-1726), Italian aristocrat and military commander who supported Felipe V during the War of Spanish Succession. His palace stood nearby.

name: Eugenia de Montijo
etymology_summary: Named after Eugenia de Montijo (1826-1920), Countess of Teba and Empress of France as wife of Napoleon III.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenia_de_Montijo; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Guzman el Bueno
etymology_summary: Named after Alfonso Perez de Guzman 'el Bueno' (1256-1309), military strategist who famously defended Tarifa against the Moors, choosing duty over his own son's life.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guzm%C3%A1n_el_Bueno; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Alonso Martinez
etymology_summary: Named after Manuel Alonso Martinez (1827-1891), jurist and politician who authored the 1888 Spanish Civil Code.

name: Diego de Leon
etymology_summary: Named after Diego de Leon (1807-1841), a military officer and politician executed for his role in a failed pronunciamiento.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_de_Le%C3%B3n; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Vicente Aleixandre
etymology_summary: Named after Vicente Aleixandre (1898-1984), poet of the Generation of '27 who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1977. Station renamed in 2018 (formerly Metropolitano).

name: Concha Espina
etymology_summary: Named after Concha Espina (1869-1955), a prominent Spanish novelist.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concha_Espina; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Santiago Bernabeu
etymology_summary: Named after Santiago Bernabeu (1895-1978), long-serving president of Real Madrid football club. The station was renamed from 'Lima' in 1997 due to its proximity to the stadium.

name: Estacion del Arte
etymology_summary: Renamed in 2018 to reflect the station's position at the heart of Madrid's art triangle: Museo del Prado, Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza, and Museo Reina Sofia.
named_after: Barrio de las Artes (Prado-Reina Sofia-Thyssen museum triangle)

name: Feria de Madrid
etymology_summary: Renamed from 'Campo de las Naciones' in 2017 due to proximity to the IFEMA trade fair complex.

name: Estadio Metropolitano
etymology_summary: Renamed from 'Estadio Olimpico' in 2017 when Atletico Madrid moved to the Wanda Metropolitano stadium nearby.

name: Atocha
etymology_summary: From the pre-Roman word *taucia meaning 'mata/matorral' (thicket/shrubland). 'Atocha' is a synonym for esparto grass (Stipa tenacissima) per the RAE. Corominas traces it through Mozarabic *attawca* back to pre-Roman *taucia, which also produced Galician-Portuguese 'touza'. First documented in the Fuero de Madrid (1202) as 'Prato de Toia' and in 1219 as 'Tocha'. Site of Spain's first railway terminus (Madrid-Aranjuez, 1851).
source: CVC Cervantes; Corominas; eldiario.es; Fuero de Madrid 1202

name: Piramides
etymology_summary: Named after two 14-metre obelisks ('piramides') built in 1831 by architect Francisco Javier de Marietegui at the entrance to the Puente de Toledo. Despite being obelisks rather than pyramids, they gave the area its name. The glorieta was formally named 'Glorieta de Piramides' on 28 December 1944; before that it was 'Glorieta del Puente de Toledo'.
named_after: Obelisks at Puente de Toledo (1831, by Francisco Javier de Marietegui)
source: Mirador Madrid; Wikipedia; El Diario de Madrid

name: Tribunal
etymology_summary: Named after the Tribunal de Cuentas (Court of Auditors), built in 1863, located on the street above. Originally called Hospicio after the nearby Royal Hospice orphanage (1726).

name: Noviciado
etymology_summary: Named after the Jesuit novitiate (Noviciado de la Compania de Jesus) that stood on Calle San Bernardo. The building later became the Universidad Central.

name: Bilbao
etymology_summary: Named after the Glorieta de Bilbao roundabout, which honours the Basque city of Bilbao. The glorieta was a historic boundary point of northern Madrid.

name: Quevedo
etymology_summary: Named after the Glorieta de Quevedo, honouring Francisco de Quevedo (1580-1645), one of Spain's greatest Golden Age poets and satirists.

name: Islas Filipinas
etymology_summary: Named after the Philippine Islands (Islas Filipinas), former Spanish colony. The nearby Avenida de Filipinas was named to honour the archipelago's colonial connection to Spain.

name: Moncloa
etymology_summary: Named after the Moncloa area. The name derives from 'Mons Clovis' (Latin for Mount of Clovis), referencing the Frankish king. Linked to the Castillo de la Monclova estate in Seville.

name: Ventas
etymology_summary: Named after Las Ventas, the area where the famous Plaza de Toros de Las Ventas bullring (1931) is located. 'Ventas' refers to the roadside inns that once dotted this area.

name: Manuel Becerra
etymology_summary: Named after Manuel Becerra Bermudez (1820-1896), mathematician, engineer, and politician who served as minister under Amadeo I and Alfonso XII. He was also Grand Master of the Grand Orient of Spain.

name: O'Donnell
etymology_summary: Named after Calle O'Donnell, honouring Leopoldo O'Donnell (1809-1867), 1st Duke of Tetuan, general and prime minister of Spain. The street was named when Madrid's walls were torn down in 1868.

name: Ibiza
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Ibiza, which references the Balearic island of Ibiza. The street naming is linked to the Dukes of Medinaceli who held properties on the island.

name: Pacifico
etymology_summary: Named after the former Calle del Pacifico (now Avenida de la Ciudad de Barcelona), which honoured the Spanish Navy's victories on the Pacific coast of Chile and Peru in 1865-1866.
named_after: Spanish naval campaigns in the Pacific (1865)

name: Menendez Pelayo
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Menendez Pelayo, honouring Marcelino Menendez y Pelayo (1856-1912), a renowned writer, philologist, and literary critic from Santander. Nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature.

name: Rios Rosas
etymology_summary: Named after Antonio de los Rios Rosas (1812-1873), a jurist, orator, and liberal politician from Ronda (Malaga). He was one of the most respected parliamentarians of 19th-century Spain.

name: Iglesia
etymology_summary: Named after the Iglesia de Santa Teresa y Santa Isabel, a parish church built 1842-1856 near the Glorieta de Joaquin Sorolla. The station was originally planned as 'Martinez Campos'.
named_after: Iglesia de Santa Teresa y Santa Isabel
previous_names: Martinez Campos (planned but never used); Sorolla (Civil War era)

name: Cruz del Rayo
etymology_summary: Named after the Colonia Cruz del Rayo residential area. The toponym refers to a stone cross that was struck and damaged by lightning ('rayo') at some historical point.
named_after: Cruz del Rayo (stone cross struck by lightning)

name: Prosperidad
etymology_summary: Named after the Prosperidad neighbourhood, itself named for Prospero Soynard y Polen, a 19th-century landowner who parcelled the area's properties, attracting working-class immigrants from the interior.

name: Cuatro Caminos
etymology_summary: Named after the Glorieta de Cuatro Caminos, a crossroads where four major roads converge: Bravo Murillo, Reina Victoria, Santa Engracia, and Raimundo Fernandez Villaverde.

name: Tetuan
etymology_summary: Named after the barrio of Tetuan de las Victorias, which commemorates Spain's victory in the Battle of Tetuan (1860) during the Spanish-Moroccan War led by General O'Donnell.

name: Estrecho
etymology_summary: Named after the local area which honours the Strait of Gibraltar (Estrecho de Gibraltar), continuing the neighbourhood's North African military nomenclature theme (near Tetuan).

name: Valdeacederas
etymology_summary: Named after the historical street (now Capitan Blanco Argibay). 'Valdeacederas' means 'valley of the sorrels' (Rumex acetosa), a plant that grew abundantly in the area.

name: Francos Rodriguez
etymology_summary: Named after Jose Francos Rodriguez (1862-1931), journalist, playwright, and mayor of Madrid (1910). He was also a prominent member of the Real Academia Espanola.

name: Carpetana
etymology_summary: Named after Via Carpetana, which references the Carpetani, a pre-Roman Celtic people who inhabited central Iberia including the area of modern Madrid. Paleontological remains (14 million years old) were found during station works in 2008.

name: Oporto
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Oporto, which references the Portuguese city of Porto (Oporto in Spanish). Part of Madrid's tradition of naming streets after significant European cities.

name: Vista Alegre
etymology_summary: Named after the Vista Alegre neighbourhood, which takes its name from the Quinta de Vista Alegre ('Joyful View Estate'), a royal estate purchased by Queen Maria Cristina in 1832.

name: Carabanchel
etymology_summary: Named after the Carabanchel district, formerly two independent municipalities (Alto and Bajo). The most accepted etymology traces it to the pre-Roman/Indo-European root *kar-/*karav- meaning 'stone' (per Menendez Pidal, Toponimia Prerromana Hispana 1953), describing 'stony ground'. Menendez Pidal links it to Garabandal (Cantabria) as a variant, both from *carau-*. The earliest documented form is 'Caravangiel/Caravanchel' (1 January 1181, original parchment in Archivo de la Catedral de Toledo); 'Carauanchiel' appears in 1264. Alternative theories: Arabic 'carab' (cultivable land owner, per Oliver Asin); 'garbanzal' (chickpea field -- the area was famed for excellent chickpeas); the Illyrian anthroponym Caravantius with diminutive Carabancilius (per Caridad Arias 2004). The Mozarabic variant 'Caramanchel' appears through B/M alternation.
source: Menendez Pidal, Toponimia Prerromana Hispana 1953; Caridad Arias (Anales IEM 44, 2004, pp. 821-830: dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=3012173); Oliver Asin; Archivo Catedral de Toledo (1181 doc); karabanchel.com; celtiberia.net/es/poblamientos/?id=799

name: Arturo Soria
etymology_summary: Named after Arturo Soria y Mata (1844-1920), visionary urbanist who designed the Ciudad Lineal (Linear City) concept in Madrid, a pioneering model of urban planning built 1892-1911.

name: Esperanza
etymology_summary: Named after the Esperanza housing development (colonia). The station serves the Esperanza neighbourhood in the Ciudad Lineal district.

name: Canillas
etymology_summary: Named after the historical village of Canillas, an ancient settlement annexed to Madrid in 1949. The village had an agricultural character for centuries.

name: Mar de Cristal
etymology_summary: Named after the Glorieta Mar de Cristal roundabout in the Hortaleza district. The poetic name 'Sea of Crystal' likely references the area's development.

name: Chamartin
etymology_summary: Named after the former municipality of Chamartin de la Rosa, annexed to Madrid in 1948. The name likely derives from an old estate or family name; the area was historically rural.

name: Colombia
etymology_summary: Named after the South American country of Colombia. Located in the Hispanoamerica neighbourhood where many streets are named after Latin American countries and locations.

name: Nuevos Ministerios
etymology_summary: Named after the Nuevos Ministerios government complex, designed by Secundino Zuazo Ugalde and sponsored by Minister Indalecio Prieto. Construction began 1933, completed 1942.

name: Ruben Dario
etymology_summary: Named after Ruben Dario (1867-1916), the Nicaraguan poet who founded the literary movement of Modernismo. Born Felix Ruben Garcia Sarmiento.

name: Nunez de Balboa
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Vasco Nunez de Balboa (1475-1519), the Spanish explorer who was the first European to sight the Pacific Ocean from the Americas in 1513.

name: Barajas
etymology_summary: Named after the district of Barajas, a former independent town annexed to Madrid. (1) Bar Axa theory: Philip II's 1575 Relaciones topograficas record that 'en tiempo que los moros, fue senor de este pueblo un moro llamado Baraja, hijo de una mora llamada Aja'. Covarrubias (Tesoro 1611) supports this, noting 'Axa' could be Hebrew (daughter of Caleb) or Arabic ('the adorned one'). (2) Latin *varalia* (fence of crossbars) per Nieto Ballester (1997). (3) Latin *uaralia* (quarrel/litigation) per Gutierre Tibon -- different semantic value from Nieto's proposal. (4) Pre-Roman toponym or ethnonym per Caridad Arias (Anales IEM XLVII, 2007), with parallels across the Peninsula and Gaul.
source: Philip II Relaciones topograficas 1575; Covarrubias, Tesoro de la lengua 1611; Nieto Ballester, Breve diccionario de toponimos espanoles 1997; Caridad Arias (Anales IEM XLVII, 2007); Isabel Gea; cvc.cervantes.es/foros/leer_asunto1.asp?vCodigo=45869

name: Canillejas
etymology_summary: Named after Canillejas, an ancient village founded in the 13th century and annexed to Madrid in 1949. It served as an agricultural settlement providing water and crops to Madrid for over six centuries.

name: Torre Arias
etymology_summary: Named after the Quinta de Torre Arias, a 16th-century noble estate built during the reign of Felipe II. The tower and estate passed through several aristocratic families including the Counts of Villamor and Dukes of Osuna.

name: Legazpi
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Legazpi, honouring Miguel Lopez de Legazpi (1502-1572), the Basque conquistador who led the expedition to colonise the Philippines and became the first governor-general of the Spanish East Indies.

name: Delicias
etymology_summary: Named after the Paseo de las Delicias, originally 'las Delicias del rio' (Delights of the River). The name comes from the Palace of Delicias del Rio, a historic pleasure ground near the Manzanares River. The nearby Delicias railway station (1880) is now the Railway Museum.

name: Mendez Alvaro
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco Mendez Alvaro (1806-1883), a physician, writer, and briefly mayor of Madrid in 1843. His term lasted only one month.

name: Palos de la Frontera
etymology_summary: Named after the town of Palos de la Frontera in Huelva province, from where Columbus set sail in 1492. The station was originally called 'Palos de Moguer' due to a historical error that confused the towns of Palos de la Frontera and Moguer; corrected in 1986.

name: Pavones
etymology_summary: Named after the Pavones neighbourhood in the Moratalaz district. The station is under the Calle de la Hacienda de Pavones.

name: Valdebernardo
etymology_summary: Named after the Valdebernardo neighbourhood, a relatively recent urban development in the Vicalvaro district, officially designated as a neighbourhood in 2017.

name: Vicalvaro
etymology_summary: Named after the historic town of Vicalvaro, annexed to Madrid. The town is notable for the Pronunciamiento de Vicalvaro (1854), a military uprising led by General O'Donnell.

name: San Cipriano
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de San Cipriano, honouring Saint Cyprian, a 3rd-century Christian martyr. The saint's name derives from Latin 'Cyprianus', meaning 'from Cyprus'.

name: Hospital 12 de Octubre
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, a major public hospital. The hospital's name references October 12, Spain's National Day (Dia de la Hispanidad), commemorating Columbus's arrival in America in 1492.

name: Almendrales
etymology_summary: Named after the Almendrales neighbourhood. 'Almendrales' means 'almond groves', referencing the almond trees that historically grew in this area south of Madrid.

name: Usera
etymology_summary: Named after the Usera district, which takes its name from Colonel Marcelo Usera. He married the daughter of 'Tio Sordillo', a farmer whose lands he proposed to develop into housing plots (1925-1930).

name: Plaza Eliptica
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza Eliptica roundabout, so called because of its elliptical shape. It sits at the junction of the Usera and Carabanchel districts.

name: Puerta de Arganda
etymology_summary: Named as a gateway ('puerta') to the municipality of Arganda del Rey. The station marks the boundary where the metro exits Madrid towards Arganda.

name: Arganda del Rey
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality of Arganda del Rey. The name 'Arganda' likely derives from the Indo-European root 'arg' (white/bright). 'Del Rey' was added in 1996, referencing Philip II's 1583 purchase of the town from the Archbishopric of Toledo.

name: La Poveda
etymology_summary: Named after the La Poveda neighbourhood of Arganda del Rey. 'Poveda' derives from 'alameda' (poplar grove), referencing the poplar trees (chopos) that historically grew in this area.

name: Tres Olivos
etymology_summary: Named after the Tres Olivos residential area. 'Tres Olivos' means 'Three Olive Trees', a toponym referencing olive trees that marked the location.

name: Montecarmelo
etymology_summary: Named after the PAU (urban development) of Montecarmelo. 'Monte Carmelo' references Mount Carmel, a mountain range in Israel sacred to the Carmelite religious order.

name: Las Tablas
etymology_summary: Named after the PAU of Las Tablas, a modern residential development. 'Las Tablas' means 'The Boards/Planks', likely a rural toponym referencing flat terrain or wooden structures.

name: Pinar de Chamartin
etymology_summary: Named after the pine grove ('pinar') that was part of the former municipality of Chamartin de la Rosa. The area retains its name from the historical wooded landscape.
named_after: Pinar de Chamartin (pine grove of Chamartin)

name: Anton Martin
etymology_summary: Named after Anton Martin de Dios (1500-1553), a Spanish religious figure and nurse who founded the Hospital de San Juan de Dios at this location in 1552.

name: Retiro
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque del Buen Retiro (Park of the Pleasant Retreat), created in the 1630s as a royal pleasure ground for King Felipe IV by the Count-Duke of Olivares.

name: Banco de Espana
etymology_summary: Named after the Bank of Spain building (1891), the country's central bank, located adjacent to the station at Plaza de Cibeles.

name: Sevilla
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de Sevilla, a street referencing the Andalusian city of Seville. The station sits at the intersection of Calle de Alcala and Calle de Sevilla.

name: Santo Domingo
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Santo Domingo, which references the Dominican convent of Santo Domingo el Real that stood nearby from the 13th century until its demolition in 1869.
named_after: Convento de Santo Domingo el Real

name: San Bernardo
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de San Bernardo, which references Saint Bernard of Clairvaux. A Cistercian monastery dedicated to him once stood on this street.

name: Canal
etymology_summary: Named after the Canal de Isabel II water infrastructure. The station is near the Third Reservoir of the Canal de Isabel II, Madrid's water supply system inaugurated in 1858 under Queen Isabel II.

name: Ventura Rodriguez
etymology_summary: Named after Ventura Rodriguez Tizon (1717-1785), one of Spain's most important 18th-century architects. He worked on the Palacio Real and designed numerous churches and public buildings in Madrid.

name: Puerta de Toledo
etymology_summary: Named after the Puerta de Toledo, the last monumental gate built in Madrid (completed 1827). It was designed as a triumphal arch by Antonio Lopez Aguado, originally conceived during the Napoleonic occupation.

name: Acacias
etymology_summary: Named after the Paseo de las Acacias (Acacia Walk), a promenade lined with acacia trees in the Arganzuela district.

name: Marques de Vadillo
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco Antonio de Salcedo y Aguirre (c.1660-1729), 1st Marques de Vadillo, the corregidor (chief magistrate) of Madrid who commissioned the Puente de Toledo bridge, designed by Pedro de Ribera.
named_after: Francisco Antonio de Salcedo y Aguirre

name: Conde de Casal
etymology_summary: Named after Manuel Escriva de Romani y de la Quintana (1871-1954), Count of Casal, a lawyer, politician, senator, and ceramics historian who served in the Madrid city council.

name: Sainz de Baranda
etymology_summary: Named after Pedro Sainz de Baranda y Gorriti (1775-1855), considered Madrid's first constitutional mayor (alcalde). He led the city government during the War of Independence and the Liberal Triennium.

name: Serrano
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Serrano, honouring Francisco Serrano y Dominguez (1810-1885), regent of Spain and general. The street was named after the 1868 revolution.

name: Velazquez
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Velazquez, honouring Diego Velazquez (1599-1660), the great Spanish painter of the Baroque period, famous for 'Las Meninas'.

name: Lista
etymology_summary: Named after Alberto Lista y Aragon (1775-1848), a mathematician, poet, journalist, and literary critic from Seville. The original street name was changed to Jose Ortega y Gasset in 1955 but the station kept the name.

name: Colon
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Colon, honouring Christopher Columbus (Cristobal Colon), the explorer who reached the Americas in 1492. A 17-metre marble monument (1885) stands in the plaza.

name: Republica Argentina
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de la Republica Argentina, honouring Argentina. Part of the Hispanoamerica neighbourhood where streets are named after Latin American countries.

name: Alonso Cano
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Alonso Cano, honouring Alonso Cano (1601-1667), a painter, sculptor, and architect from Granada, known as the 'Spanish Michelangelo'.

name: Cuzco
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Cuzco, which honours the Peruvian city of Cusco (Cuzco), the historic capital of the Inca Empire. Part of the Latin American naming theme in the Hispanoamerica neighbourhood.

name: Plaza de Castilla
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Castilla, a major square at the northern end of Paseo de la Castellana. Named after the historic Crown of Castile.

name: Alvarado
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Alvarado, honouring Pedro de Alvarado (c.1485-1541), a Spanish conquistador and captain under Hernan Cortes during the conquest of Mexico and Central America.

name: Puente de Vallecas
etymology_summary: Named after the Puente de Vallecas district, which references the bridge ('puente') built over the Abroñigal stream that connected Madrid to the Vallecas area.

name: Nueva Numancia
etymology_summary: Named after the Nueva Numancia neighbourhood. In 1873 residents petitioned to declare it an independent town named 'Nueva Numancia' after the legendary Celtiberian city of Numancia that resisted Roman siege (133 BC).

name: Portazgo
etymology_summary: Named after the local area, which references a medieval 'portazgo' (road toll) on the Valencia road at Vallecas. Portazgos were taxes charged for using newly constructed roads.

name: Puerta del Angel
etymology_summary: Named after the Puerta del Angel neighbourhood. The name originates from a 1605 ermita built to house an angel figure rescued from the Puerta de Guadalajara after it burned in 1582.

name: Alto de Extremadura
etymology_summary: Named after its elevated location ('alto') along the road to Extremadura (Paseo de Extremadura), the historic route from Madrid to the Extremadura region of western Spain.

name: Lucero
etymology_summary: Named after the Lucero neighbourhood in the Latina district. 'Lucero' means 'bright star' or 'morning star' in Spanish.

name: Laguna
etymology_summary: Named after the Laguna neighbourhood. 'Laguna' means 'lagoon' or 'small lake', likely referencing a former body of water in the area.

name: Aluche
etymology_summary: Named after the Aluche neighbourhood. The name is believed to derive from the Luche stream ('Arroyo de Luche') that ran through the area. Maps noted it as 'A. Luche' (Arroyo Luche), which evolved into 'Aluche'.

name: Campamento
etymology_summary: Named after the Campamento neighbourhood, which references the military camps ('campamentos') that were established in the area. The name dates to 1885 when the mayor of Carabanchel Alto designated the area.

name: Batan
etymology_summary: Named after the Venta del Batan, a historical inn associated with the bull pens ('corrales') where fighting bulls were kept before fights. 'Batan' refers to a fulling mill.

name: Lago
etymology_summary: Named after the lake ('lago') in the Casa de Campo park, a large artificial lake near this entrance to the park.
named_after: Lago de la Casa de Campo (lake)

name: Casa de Campo
etymology_summary: Named after the Casa de Campo, Madrid's largest public park (1722 hectares). Originally a royal hunting estate acquired by Felipe II in 1562, it was opened to the public in 1931.

name: Plaza de Espana
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Espana, one of Madrid's major squares featuring monuments to Cervantes and his literary characters Don Quijote and Sancho Panza.

name: Ciudad Universitaria
etymology_summary: Named after Madrid's Ciudad Universitaria (University City), home to the Universidad Complutense de Madrid, the Polytechnic University, and UNED. The campus was planned in the 1920s under Alfonso XIII.

name: Pio XII
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Pio XII, honouring Pope Pius XII (Eugenio Pacelli, 1876-1958), who was head of the Catholic Church from 1939 to 1958.

name: Duque de Pastrana
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza Duque de Pastrana. The Duchy of Pastrana was created in 1572 by Felipe II for Ruy Gomez de Silva, Prince of Eboli. The area's naming reflects the historical presence of the ducal estate.
named_after: Ruy Gomez de Silva (1st Duke of Pastrana)

name: Herrera Oria
etymology_summary: Named after Angel Herrera Oria (1886-1968), journalist, educator, Catholic social activist, and priest. He founded the newspaper El Debate and the Catholic Association of Propagandists.

name: Barrio del Pilar
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio del Pilar neighbourhood, which references the Virgen del Pilar (Our Lady of the Pillar), one of Spain's most important Catholic devotions, patron of Zaragoza.

name: Ventilla
etymology_summary: Named after the Ventilla neighbourhood. 'Ventilla' is a diminutive of 'venta' (inn/tavern), suggesting there was a small roadside inn at this location.

name: Mirasierra
etymology_summary: Named after the Mirasierra neighbourhood, meaning 'Mountain View' - referring to the views of the Sierra de Guadarrama visible from the area. The colonia was founded c.1927-1950 as a residential development.

name: Arganzuela-Planetario
etymology_summary: Named after the Arganzuela district and the Planetario de Madrid (planetarium), located in the nearby Parque Tierno Galvan. Opened in 2007 within an already-operating line.

name: Suanzes
etymology_summary: Named after Juan Antonio Suanzes Fernandez (1891-1977), naval engineer, first president of the Instituto Nacional de Industria (INI), and Minister of Industry under Franco. He was posthumously honoured with the Marquis of Suanzes title in 1960.

name: Ciudad Lineal
etymology_summary: Named after the Ciudad Lineal district, which takes its name from Arturo Soria's pioneering 'Linear City' urban planning concept (1892-1911).

name: Quintana
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Quintana in the Ciudad Lineal district. The Quintana neighbourhood was developed as part of the broader urban expansion of eastern Madrid.

name: El Carmen
etymology_summary: Named after the El Carmen neighbourhood, which likely references the Virgen del Carmen (Our Lady of Mount Carmel), a widely venerated figure in Spanish Catholicism.

name: Garcia Noblejas
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de los Hermanos Garcia Noblejas, referencing the Garcia-Noblejas brothers, a family of five Falangist members during the Spanish Civil War. The naming is politically controversial.

name: Simancas
etymology_summary: Named after the Simancas neighbourhood, which references the Castilian town of Simancas (Valladolid), famous for the Battle of Simancas (939) and the General Archive of Simancas.

name: Las Musas
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Musas neighbourhood, referencing the Muses of Greek mythology. The area was a residential colony (colonia) in the Canillejas zone with mythological and classical street names.

name: San Blas
etymology_summary: Named after the San Blas neighbourhood, honouring Saint Blaise, a 4th-century Armenian bishop and martyr who is the patron saint of throat ailments.

name: Pueblo Nuevo
etymology_summary: Named after the Pueblo Nuevo neighbourhood, meaning 'New Town'. The area developed as a new settlement on the outskirts of Madrid in the 19th-20th centuries.

name: Pinar del Rey
etymology_summary: Named after the Pinar del Rey neighbourhood, meaning 'King's Pine Grove', referencing a historical royal pine forest in the Hortaleza district.

name: Bambú
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle Bambu in the Chamartin district. The street name references the bamboo plant, part of a botanical naming theme in the neighbourhood.

name: Estrella
etymology_summary: Named after the Estrella neighbourhood in the Retiro district. The station is located beneath the M-30 motorway near the Calle Estrella Polar.

name: Vinateros
etymology_summary: Named after the Camino de Vinateros, an old path used by wine merchants ('vinateros') who transported wine through this area south of Madrid.

name: Artilleros
etymology_summary: Named after the Pico de Artilleros, referencing artillerymen ('artilleros'). The military name reflects the historical presence of military installations in the area.

name: Avenida de America
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de America, a major avenue in Madrid named to honour the Americas. The station is a major multimodal transport hub.

name: Cartagena
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Cartagena, referencing the historic port city of Cartagena in the Murcia region of southeastern Spain.

name: Antonio Machado
etymology_summary: Named after Antonio Machado (1875-1939), one of Spain's greatest poets of the Generation of '98. His most famous work is 'Campos de Castilla'. He died in exile in Collioure, France.

name: Valdezarza
etymology_summary: Named after the Valdezarza neighbourhood in the Moncloa-Aravaca district. 'Valdezarza' likely derives from 'valle de zarza' (bramble valley), referencing wild blackberry bushes in the area.

name: Colonia Jardin
etymology_summary: Named after the Colonia Jardin housing development, a 'garden colony' (colonia jardin) inspired by the early 20th-century garden city movement promoting green residential spaces.

name: Opanel
etymology_summary: Named after the Opanel neighbourhood in Carabanchel, which takes its name from the Arroyo de Opanel, a stream that once flowed through the area before being buried during urbanisation. The toponym may have pre-Roman hydronymic origins: the prefix 'Op-' could relate to the root *up-/*op- meaning 'water/river' found in pre-Roman Hispanic toponymy (per Villar Liebana, Palaeohispanica 2002). The station originally opened as 'Elvas' in 1981 but was renamed 'Opanel' in 1984 at residents' request.
source: Villar Liebana, 'Los toponimos con *up- (*op-) agua, rio', Palaeohispanica 2 (2002) pp. 277-291 (dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=670065; ifc.dpz.es/recursos/publicaciones/21/92/14villar.pdf); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Opanel; karabanchel.com

name: Rivas Vaciamadrid
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality of Rivas-Vaciamadrid. 'Rivas' comes from Guillermo Rivas, an 11th-century military founder. 'Vaciamadrid' derives from Arabic 'Fahs al-Mayrit' (field of Madrid).

name: Julian Besteiro
etymology_summary: Named after Julian Besteiro Fernandez (1870-1940), a university professor and socialist politician. He served as president of the Spanish Parliament (Cortes Constituyentes) from 1931-1933 during the Second Republic, and was president of both the PSOE and UGT. Educated at the Institucion Libre de Ensenanza and the Sorbonne, he led the moderate wing of Spanish socialism. He died in Carmona prison after being sentenced by a Francoist court martial.

name: Juan de la Cierva
etymology_summary: Named after Juan de la Cierva y Codorniu (1895-1936), the Spanish civil engineer and aviator from Murcia who invented the autogiro (autogyro), the precursor to the modern helicopter. His C.4 prototype achieved the first successful flight of a stable rotary-wing aircraft in 1923. He died in a KLM plane crash at Croydon Airport, London.

name: Alonso de Mendoza
etymology_summary: Named after Alonso de Mendoza y Nunez de Prado (d. c. 1507), a steward (mayordomo) of Archbishop Alfonso Carrillo de Albornoz who served as mayor of Bonilla de la Sierra. In his 1507 will, he bequeathed nearly all his assets to found the Hospital de San Jose in Getafe, one of Spain's oldest continuously operating charitable foundations, serving the poor of Getafe, Pinto, and Grinon.
named_after: Alonso de Mendoza y Nunez de Prado

name: Hospital Severo Ochoa
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario Severo Ochoa in Leganes, which is itself named after Severo Ochoa de Albornoz (1905-1993), the Asturian biochemist who won the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the enzymes involved in RNA synthesis. The hospital's construction began in 1981, opened partially in 1987, and was officially inaugurated in 1988 with Severo Ochoa himself attending.

name: Reyes Catolicos
etymology_summary: Named after the Reyes Catolicos (Catholic Monarchs): Queen Isabella I of Castile (1451-1504) and King Ferdinand II of Aragon (1452-1516), who unified Spain and sponsored Columbus's voyage.
named_after: Reyes Catolicos (Isabella I and Ferdinand II)

name: Manuel de Falla
etymology_summary: Named after Manuel de Falla (1876-1946), one of Spain's most important classical composers, known for works like 'Noches en los Jardines de Espana' and 'El Amor Brujo'.

name: Marqués de la Valdavia
etymology_summary: Named after the Marques de la Valdavia, a noble title associated with the Alcobendas area. The title was held by local landowners with significant historical presence in the municipality.

name: Avenida de la Paz
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de la Paz, the eastern section of the M-30 ring road built along the former Abroñigal stream bed. The avenue was inaugurated in 1974 and named in allusion to peace, likely referencing the post-Civil War era. Officially denominated in 1991.
named_after: Avenida de la Paz (M-30 eastern section)

name: San Lorenzo
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio de San Lorenzo and its parish. San Lorenzo (Saint Lawrence of Rome, 225-258) was a deacon of Rome martyred on a gridiron. Patron saint of numerous Spanish localities.

name: Parque de Santa Maria
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque de Santa María neighbourhood in Hortaleza, which takes its name from the Parroquia Santa María del Parque (Parish of Saint Mary of the Park) established in the 1970s. The neighbourhood was built in the 1960s by the developer Construcciones Residenciales y Sociales.

name: Hortaleza
etymology_summary: Named after the district of Hortaleza, a former independent village annexed to Madrid in 1950. The name derives from the Latin 'hortus' (garden/orchard), referring to the abundant vegetable gardens historically cultivated in the area, though some theories suggest it derives from 'fortaleza' (fortress).

name: Manoteras
etymology_summary: Named after the area of Manoteras, first documented in 1807 as 'Las Manoteras'. According to philologist Emilio Nieto Ballester, the name derives from Latin 'lumba altaria' (high hills), evolving through 'Lomaotera' to 'La Manotera', describing the elevated terrain between Fuencarral and Hortaleza.

name: Empalme
etymology_summary: Named after the railway junction ('empalme' means junction/connection) between the Madrid-Almorox line and the F.C. Suburbano de Carabanchel, which crossed here. An apeadero called Empalme-Goya was established to connect both rail systems.

name: Urgel
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de Urgel, referencing the city and former Condado de Urgell (Urgel) in Catalonia (Lleida), one of the most important medieval Catalan counties.

name: El Capricho
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque de El Capricho, a romantic garden created between 1787 and 1839 by María Josefa Pimentel, Duchess of Osuna. 'El Capricho' (The Caprice/Whim) was the name the duchess gave to her pleasure estate, also linked to Goya's famous 'Caprichos' etchings which the dukes collected.

name: Alameda de Osuna
etymology_summary: Named after the Alameda de Osuna neighbourhood. 'Alameda' means poplar-lined promenade and 'Osuna' refers to the Dukes of Osuna who owned a large estate here including the famous El Capricho garden. Particularly María Josefa Pimentel (1752-1834) XII Countess-Duchess of Benavente.

name: Pitis
etymology_summary: Named after the Pitis area in Fuencarral-El Pardo district, a pre-existing rural place name documented well before the railway station opened in 1964. The exact origin is genuinely unknown -- the FilobLogos blog on Madrid natural toponymy (2007) explicitly lists Pitis among names for which 'no se saben' (are not known). One speculative hypothesis links it to Greek 'Pitys' (pine), a nymph transformed into a pine tree, paralleling the Pitiusas islands etymology; the nearby neighbourhood is called 'Pinar' (pine grove). No scholarly source has treated this toponym. A shantytown of ~150 mostly Portuguese families grew around the station until demolition c. 2005. Campaigns to rename to 'Arroyo del Fresno' or 'Miguel de Cervantes' (2016) failed.

name: Arroyofresno
etymology_summary: Named after the Arroyo del Fresno (Ash Tree Stream) residential area. The name combines 'arroyo' (stream) and 'fresno' (ash tree) describing the natural landscape of a stream lined with ash trees that historically flowed through this part of northern Madrid.

name: Lacoma
etymology_summary: Named after Margarita González Lacoma (1896-1976) a Spanish businesswoman from Burgos who founded Casa Lacoma a haute couture fashion house on Gran Vía in 1925. She later became a real estate developer building the Colonia Lacoma workers' housing development in this area in the 1940s-50s.

name: Avenida de la Ilustracion
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de la Ilustracion ('Avenue of the Enlightenment'), referencing the 18th-century intellectual movement especially influential in Spain under Carlos III (1759-1788).

name: Peñagrande
etymology_summary: Named after the Peñagrande neighbourhood meaning 'Large Rock'. The name references a prominent large rock formation that for centuries served as a landmark for shepherds and inhabitants of the area. The colony of Peñagrande originated in 1914 as 'Colonia El Porvenir-Fuente la Mina'.

name: Parque de las Avenidas
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque de las Avenidas (Park of the Avenues) a park designed by architect Cecilio Rodríguez and built between 1928 and 1933. The name refers to the major avenues that define the surrounding neighbourhood's layout particularly Avenida de Bruselas and other European city-named streets.

name: Barrio de la Concepcion
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio de la Concepción which originated as the 'Colonia Agrícola La Purísima Concepción' (Agricultural Colony of the Immaculate Conception) in the 19th century. The name refers to the Catholic dogma of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary later reinforced by the local parish.

name: Ascao
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de Ascao in Pueblo Nuevo, Ciudad Lineal. The street name derives from Ascao/Askao, a historic neighbourhood in Bilbao's Old Town (Casco Viejo). The Madrid street follows a Basque-origin naming pattern: the adjacent Barrio de Bilbao was founded by a wealthy Basque family, and its streets were named after places in the province of Vizcaya. The Basque toponym 'Askao' is composed of 'aska' (manger/watering trough/ditch) + 'ao' (mouth), referring to the horseshoe shape of the Bilbao estuary.
source: Aunamendi Eusko Entziklopedia; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pueblo_Nuevo_(Ciudad_Lineal); Irigoien etymology; fgacedo.blogspot.com

name: Barrio del Puerto
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio del Puerto neighbourhood in Coslada. The name references the nearby Puerto Seco (Dry Port) de Coslada a major inland logistics platform established in 1995-2001 that connects with Spain's four largest seaports.

name: Coslada Central
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the centre of Coslada municipality. 'Coslada' has disputed etymology: possibly from Latin 'cos' (flint) + 'late' (abundant) or from Celtic 'coslo/cosla' (hazelnut) or from Latin 'cova ustulata' (burnt cave). The town dates back to at least 1083.

name: La Rambla
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de la Rambla in Coslada. 'Rambla' derives from Arabic 'ramla' (sandy riverbed/seasonal watercourse). In urban planning, a wide tree-lined promenade.
named_after: La Rambla neighbourhood (Coslada, from Arabic ramla: sandy riverbed)

name: San Fernando
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality of San Fernando de Henares which honours Saint Ferdinand III of Castile (1199-1252). King Fernando VI who founded the town's Real Fábrica de Paños (Royal Cloth Factory) in the 1740s named it after his patron saint Ferdinand III canonized in 1671.

name: Jarama
etymology_summary: Named after the nearby Jarama River the longest and most voluminous river crossing the Madrid region. The river name has disputed origins: possibly from an Indo-European root *sar- (to flow) modified during Islamic rule; or from Berber meaning 'border river'; or from 'jara' (rockrose shrub).

name: Henares
etymology_summary: Named after the Henares River near whose course the station is located. The name derives from Spanish 'henar' (field of hay/heno) the plural form describing the hay fields historically cultivated along the river's banks. The river was known as Guadalajara during Arab rule.

name: Hospital del Henares
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario del Henares a public hospital in Coslada that opened simultaneously with the metro station in February 2008. The hospital is named after the Henares River that flows through the Corredor del Henares region.

name: Buenos Aires
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de Buenos Aires, which references the capital of Argentina. Part of a Latin American-themed street naming pattern in the Vallecas area.

name: Alto del Arenal
etymology_summary: Named after the Alto del Arenal neighbourhood. 'Alto' means 'high ground/hill'; 'arenal' means 'sandy ground'. Describes the elevated sandy terrain of this area east of Vallecas.

name: Miguel Hernandez
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Miguel Hernandez Gilabert (1910-1942), one of Spain's greatest 20th-century poets. Associated with the Generation of '36, he died in a Francoist prison of tuberculosis. Author of 'El rayo que no cesa' and 'Viento del pueblo'.

name: Sierra de Guadalupe
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle Sierra de Guadalupe, referencing the Sierra de Guadalupe mountain range in Extremadura (Caceres). The Monastery of Guadalupe, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is located there.

name: Villa de Vallecas
etymology_summary: Named after the historic Villa de Vallecas, independent until annexed by Madrid in 1950. 'Vallecas' etymology debated: possibly from Latin 'vallis' + Arab personal name 'Kas', or from 'Vallis Egas' (Valley of Egas). First documented in 1202.

name: Congosto
etymology_summary: Named after the surrounding neighbourhood. 'Congosto' derives from Latin 'coangustus' (narrow/constricted), meaning a gorge or narrow pass between terrain features. The prefix 'co-' (together) with 'angustus' (narrow) evokes two terrain elements closing to create a tight passage. A frequent toponym across Spain for narrow river gorges or defile passages, historically exploited for mills and water infrastructure.

name: La Gavia
etymology_summary: Named after the Arroyo de La Gavia, a tributary of the Manzanares flowing through Villa de Vallecas. 'Gavia' derives from Latin 'cavea' (cavity), meaning a drainage ditch or trench dug in the earth. The Cerro de La Gavia is an important archaeological site with occupations from the Paleolithic through the Iron Age Carpetano settlement (4th century BC) to Late Antiquity. The Carpetanos chose this defensive position between ravines near the stream confluence.
named_after: Arroyo de La Gavia (from Latin cavea, drainage ditch)

name: Valdecarros
etymology_summary: Named after the Valdecarros area in Villa de Vallecas. Traditionally interpreted as 'Valle de Carros' (Valley of Carts), referring to the route through this valley used by merchandise carts. An alternative theory derives it from 'Valle de Navarros' (Valley of the Navarrese), referring to Navarrese resettlers granted land here during the late 12th-century Reconquista repopulation campaigns. A parallel toponym Valdecarros exists in Salamanca province (also founded during medieval repopulation), strengthening the Navarrese theory. Earliest documented mention: 21 April 1296, in a purchase and sale document. Part of a rich cluster of Val(de)- toponyms in Vallecas: Valdeculebras, Valderribas, Valdemingomez, Valdeolmos.
named_after: Valdecarros (Valley of Carts or Valley of the Navarrese)

name: Las Rosas
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Rosas neighbourhood. 'Las Rosas' (The Roses) likely references a former estate or garden with rose bushes. The neighbourhood developed rapidly from the 1980s as part of Madrid's eastern expansion.

name: Avenida de Guadalajara
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Guadalajara, the major road leading northeast toward the city of Guadalajara. 'Guadalajara' derives from Arabic 'Wadi al-Hijara' (river of stones/valley of fortresses).

name: Alsacia
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Alsacia (Alsace Square), referencing the historical region of Alsace in northeastern France. Part of a European geography-themed naming pattern in this area of San Blas.

name: La Almudena
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de la Almudena, referencing the Virgen de la Almudena, patron saint of Madrid. 'Almudena' derives from Arabic 'al-mudayna' (the small citadel), where her image was reportedly hidden during the Moorish period.

name: La Elipa
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio de la Elipa. The name derives from 'Phelipa' or 'Felipa', referring to Phelipa de Vargas, a 13th-century noblewoman who owned lands in this area east of Madrid. Over centuries, 'tierra de la Phelipa' was shortened and corrupted to 'la Elipa'. This etymology is documented in historical land records and supported by Madrid toponymy scholars including Aparisi Laporta.
source: Aparisi Laporta, Toponimia madrilena (2001); madridnofrills.com; research on medieval land records

name: San Fermin-Orcasur
etymology_summary: 'San Fermin' references the Barrio de San Fermin, named after Saint Fermin of Amiens (3rd century), first bishop of Pamplona. 'Orcasur' is a contraction of 'Orcasitas Sur'. 'Orcasitas' possibly from 'horca' (gallows) or a family name.

name: Ciudad de los Angeles
etymology_summary: Named after the neighbourhood, which was named via a popular contest in 1958 due to its proximity to the Cerro de los Angeles (Hill of the Angels) in Getafe, the geographic and symbolic centre of the Iberian Peninsula. Built in the 1950s-60s as a satellite city for immigrant workers. Streets were named after zarzuelas (Spanish light operas) in 1983.
named_after: Cerro de los Angeles (geographic centre of Iberian Peninsula)

name: Villaverde Bajo-Cruce
etymology_summary: 'Villaverde' = 'green village', from Latin 'villa viridis'. 'Bajo' = 'lower' (vs Alto). 'Cruce' = 'crossing/junction', referring to the railway crossing. Villaverde was independent until annexed by Madrid in 1954.

name: San Cristobal
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio de San Cristobal, honouring Saint Christopher (San Cristobal), patron saint of travellers. The neighbourhood is an industrial area of Villaverde.

name: Villaverde Alto
etymology_summary: 'Villaverde' = 'green village', from Latin 'villa viridis'. 'Alto' = 'upper/high'. This was the historic centre of the former municipality of Villaverde, annexed by Madrid in 1954.

name: Penagrande
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio de Penagrande. 'Pena' = rock/crag; 'grande' = large. Describes a prominent large rock formation that characterized this area before urbanization.

name: Aeropuerto T1-T2-T3
etymology_summary: Named after terminals 1, 2, and 3 of Aeropuerto Adolfo Suarez Madrid-Barajas. 'Barajas' possibly from Arabic 'baraya' (tower/lookout). Airport renamed in 2014 after PM Adolfo Suarez.

name: Aeropuerto T4
etymology_summary: Named after Terminal 4 of Madrid-Barajas airport. T4 was designed by Richard Rogers and Antonio Lamela, opening in 2006. One of the world's largest airport terminals.

name: Rivas-Urbanizaciones
etymology_summary: Named after the urbanizaciones (housing estates) of Rivas-Vaciamadrid. These planned suburban communities grew rapidly from the 1990s.

name: Rivas Futura
etymology_summary: Named after the 'Rivas Futura' urban development in Rivas-Vaciamadrid. 'Futura' (future) reflects the forward-looking vision of this 21st-century residential area.

name: Puerta del Sur
etymology_summary: Named 'Puerta del Sur' (Southern Gate) as the station serves as the gateway connecting the Madrid Metro network (Line 10) with the MetroSur circular line. The name reflects its role as the entry point to southern Madrid's metro system from the city center.
source: Metro de Madrid; Wikipedia; alcorcon.org; crtm.es; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Puerta_del_Sur

name: Joaquin Vilumbrales
etymology_summary: Named after Joaquin Vilumbrales, former mayor of Alcorcon who died in 1999 shortly after taking office. Originally planned as 'Los Castillos'.

name: Cuatro Vientos
etymology_summary: Named after the Cuatro Vientos area. The toponym ('Four Winds') predates the aerodrome and refers to the geographic characteristic of this open, elevated plain where winds blow from all four cardinal directions. The exposed, flat terrain later made it ideal for aviation: in 1911 a military commission proposed acquiring the lands for Spain's first military aerodrome, birthplace of Spanish aviation.
source: nosolometro; Wikipedia; Real Aero Club de Espana

name: Aviacion Espanola
etymology_summary: Named in homage to the nearby Madrid-Cuatro Vientos Airport, the oldest aerodrome in Spain (founded 1911) and birthplace of Spanish aviation. Key milestones at Cuatro Vientos include the first military aerodrome (1911), first Spanish wind tunnel (1921, by Emilio Herrera), and Herrera's spacesuit prototype (1935) later studied by NASA.
source: Wikipedia; Aviacion Digital; Comunidad de Madrid

name: Begona
etymology_summary: Named after the Colonia Virgen de Begona residential development near Hospital La Paz. The Virgin of Begona is patroness of Bilbao and Biscay. 'Begona' from Basque 'beg-oina' (place at foot of the hill).

name: Fuencarral
etymology_summary: Named after the historic town of Fuencarral, independent until 1950. 'Fuencarral' from 'fuente' (spring) + 'carral' (road for carts). Literally 'spring on the cart road'.

name: Ronda de la Comunicacion
etymology_summary: Named after the road surrounding the Distrito Telefonica corporate campus. Telefonica financed the station's construction. Not in the original MetroNorte project.
named_after: Ronda de la Comunicacion (ring road at Telefonica campus)

name: La Granja
etymology_summary: Named after a street in the Vereda del Pobre industrial park of Alcobendas. 'La Granja' = 'the farm'. Originally planned as 'Alcobendas Industrial'.

name: La Moraleja
etymology_summary: Named after the La Moraleja luxury residential area of Alcobendas. 'Moraleja' is a diminutive collective of 'mora' (mulberry), meaning 'place of mulberry trees'. Originally a royal hunting estate under Carlos III.

name: Baunatal
etymology_summary: Named after the city of Baunatal in Hesse, Germany, twin city of San Sebastian de los Reyes since 1990. An unusual case of a Madrid metro station named after a German city.
source: Wikipedia; Ayto. San Sebastian de los Reyes

name: Hospital Infanta Sofia
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario Infanta Sofia, honouring Infanta Sofia of Spain (born 2007). Originally 'Hospital del Norte' until August 2008. Northern terminus of Line 10.

name: La Fortuna
etymology_summary: Named after the La Fortuna neighbourhood of Leganes, founded 1960 by developer Domingo dos Santos. Named after his deceased wife Fortunata Gonzalez Arroyo. First residents were 33 families relocated from Orcasitas.

name: La Peseta
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de la Peseta, honouring Spain's former currency (1869-2002). 'Peseta' is a diminutive of 'peso'. Residents requested 'Salvador Allende' but 'La Peseta' was chosen.

name: Carabanchel Alto
etymology_summary: Upper part of former Carabanchel municipality (annexed 1948). 'Carabanchel' etymology debated: possibly Celtic 'kar-' (stone) + suffix, or Arabic, or a personal name. 'Alto' = upper.

name: San Francisco
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de San Francisco and historic Franciscan presence. Saint Francis of Assisi (c.1181-1226), founder of the Franciscan order.

name: Pan Bendito
etymology_summary: Named after the Pan Bendito neighbourhood in Carabanchel. 'Pan Bendito' (blessed bread) is a traditional toponym predating the modern housing development, likely referring to the religious custom of distributing blessed bread in church. The area was formerly wheat fields (campos de trigo), making a bread-related name fitting. The Unidad Vecinal de Absorcion was built 1957-1963 as provisional housing for rural migrants from Andalucia and Extremadura.

name: Abrantes
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Abrantes, referencing the Duques de Abrantes, a Spanish noble title. The Palacio de Abrantes in Madrid (now Italian Cultural Institute) was acquired by the Dukes in 1842. Title originates from the Portuguese city of Abrantes.

name: Parque Lisboa
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque de Lisboa (Lisbon Park) and surrounding neighbourhood in Alcorcon. The neighbourhood's streets follow a theme of Portuguese and European city names, including Avenida de Lisboa. The park and neighbourhood were developed as part of Alcorcon's urban expansion linking the city centre with Valderas.

name: Alcorcon Central
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the centre of Alcorcon. Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2007) favours a hybrid Latin+Arabic formation: the al- prefix is a superstrate adoption over Latin *corcu/qorq from 'quercus' (oak), parallel to 'alcornoque' (cork oak), yielding 'the oak grove'. Alternative: pure Arabic 'al-kur' (hill/mound). The folk etymology connecting it to Alcorcon's famous pottery tradition is linguistically dubious per Corominas. First documented 1208.
source: Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2007); Corominas; Ayto. Alcorcon; Wikipedia

name: Parque Oeste
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque Oeste (Western Park) commercial and residential area in western Alcorcon. The area includes a major commercial park of over 125000 m2 built in 1994-1996, and also serves the nearby Rey Juan Carlos University campus.

name: Universidad Rey Juan Carlos
etymology_summary: Named after the Universidad Rey Juan Carlos (King Juan Carlos University), founded in 1996 by the Community of Madrid. The university is named after King Juan Carlos I of Spain (b. 1938), who laid the first stone of the Mostoles campus in 1997.

name: Mostoles Central
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the centre of Mostoles. Most accepted theory: from Latin 'monisterium' (monastery), evolving Monisterium > Monsteriu > Moster > Mostel > Mosteles > Mostoles, indicating pre-Islamic Christian monasteries. A 1144 document calls it 'Turrem de Monsteles' (Tower of Mosteles). Alternatives: Latin 'mustum et olea' (grape must and olive oil), or Arabic 'Mostel' per geographer Al-Idrisi.
source: Celtiberia.net; CVC Cervantes; Ayto. Mostoles; Wikipedia

name: Pradillo
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza del Pradillo, the historic central square of Mostoles. 'Pradillo' is the diminutive of 'prado' (meadow), from Latin 'pratum'. The square has been documented since the 16th century as 'Plaza del Perezal'; by the 18th century it was known as 'Pradillo del Cano', referring to a small meadow near a water spout.
named_after: Calle del Pradillo (diminutive of prado, small meadow)

name: Hospital de Mostoles
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario de Mostoles, the public hospital it serves. The hospital was inaugurated on 25 June 1983 by Health Minister Ernest Lluch as the first county hospital in Madrid province.

name: Loranca
etymology_summary: Named after the Loranca neighbourhood in Fuenlabrada, which takes its name from the medieval aldea (village) of Loranca. The village was one of the original settlements (along with Fregacedos) whose inhabitants founded Fuenlabrada in the 14th century. The toponym 'Loranca' may derive from Arabic 'luran' (valley/ravine) or from 'loranco' (a type of tree). The modern neighbourhood was developed in the 1990s as a garden city with 12000 homes.

name: Hospital de Fuenlabrada
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario de Fuenlabrada, the public hospital it serves. The hospital was created in December 2002 and opened fully in 2004-2005. Fuenlabrada had been the largest Spanish city without its own hospital, with residents previously relying on Hospital Severo Ochoa in Leganes.

name: Parque Europa
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque Europa (Europe Park), a 17454 m2 urban park in central Fuenlabrada. The park and surrounding neighbourhood follow a European naming theme, with streets named after European countries and cities (e.g. Calle Francia, Calle Belgica). Not to be confused with the larger Parque Europa theme park in Torrejon de Ardoz.

name: Fuenlabrada Central
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the centre of Fuenlabrada. The municipality name derives from 'Fuente Labrada' (carved fountain), referring to a Moorish-era stone fountain carved in lime and mortar ('cal y canto'). The town was founded in 1375 by inhabitants of the abandoned villages of Loranca and Fregacedos, who settled near this fountain.
source: Ayto. Fuenlabrada; Wikipedia; ayto-fuenlabrada.es; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuenlabrada; memoriasfuenlabrada.blogspot.com; toponhisp.org

name: Parque de los Estados
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque de los Estados (Park of the States), a 16730 m2 park in Fuenlabrada. The neighbourhood's streets are named after Central and South American countries and cities (e.g. Calle de Venezuela, Calle de Lima), with the main Avenida de los Estados (Avenue of the States) giving the area its name. The area was formerly known as 'La Pollina'.
named_after: Parque de los Estados (park in Fuenlabrada)

name: Arroyo Culebro
etymology_summary: Named after the Arroyo Culebro (Snake Stream), a 28 km intermittent watercourse that rises in the Polvoranca lagoon in Leganes and empties into the Rio Manzanares in Getafe. 'Culebro' derives from Latin 'coluber' (snake), likely referring to the stream's serpentine, winding course through the landscape. The area has archaeological significance, with Iron Age settlements discovered along the stream.

name: Conservatorio
etymology_summary: Named after the Conservatorio Profesional de Musica de Getafe (Getafe Professional Music Conservatory), located near the station. The conservatory was inaugurated in 2000 and is part of the network of public music education centres managed by the Community of Madrid.
named_after: Real Conservatorio Superior de Musica de Madrid

name: Getafe Central
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the centre of Getafe. Etymology genuinely uncertain per Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2007). The most repeated theory derives it from Arabic 'jata' (something long) via medieval 'Xatafi', referring to the long main street along the royal road to Toledo. Philip II's 1575 Relaciones Topograficas record this tradition. Garcia Sanchez notes the Arabic origin is 'presumed based on aspect and configuration' but not verifiable. Earliest forms: Satafi/Xatafi c.1150.
source: Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2007); Philip II Relaciones Topograficas 1575; Ayto. Getafe; Wikipedia

name: El Casar
etymology_summary: Named after the El Casar neighbourhood in Getafe Norte. The toponym 'casar' is an archaic Spanish word meaning a small cluster of houses or hamlet, from the noun 'casa' (house) with suffix '-ar'. It was used historically to denote a settlement too small to be called a village. The modern neighbourhood was built in the mid-to-late 1990s.
named_after: El Casar neighbourhood (Getafe, from casar: group of houses)
source: Ayto. Getafe; Wikipedia; dle.rae.es; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Casar_(Getafe); toponhisp.org

name: Los Espartales
etymology_summary: Named after the Los Espartales neighbourhood in Getafe Norte. The toponym 'espartales' refers to fields where esparto grass (Stipa tenacissima) grew. Esparto was historically an important fibre plant used for making ropes, baskets and mats across arid southern Spain. The calcareous soils of southern Madrid naturally supported these grasslands.
named_after: Los Espartales (esparto grass fields, from espartizal)

name: El Bercial
etymology_summary: Named after the El Bercial neighbourhood in Getafe. The toponym 'bercial' likely derives from 'berceo', a type of coarse grass or esparto-like shrub, indicating uncultivated scrubland. Historical maps show the older form 'Hervestial'. The area has been inhabited since the 1950s-60s, with significant development from the 2000s onward.
named_after: El Bercial neighbourhood (Getafe, from bercial: watercress area)

name: El Carrascal
etymology_summary: Named after the El Carrascal neighbourhood in Leganes. 'Carrascal' means a place or hillside covered with 'carrascas' (small holm oaks, Quercus ilex), from the pre-Roman root 'carrasco'. The neighbourhood was developed from 1981 onward with planned urbanisation, unlike the earlier unplanned expansion of neighbouring Zarzaquemada.
named_after: El Carrascal (holm oak grove, from carrasca: Quercus ilex)
source: Ayto. Leganes; Wikipedia; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Carrascal; leganes.callejero.net; planosdemadrid.es

name: Casa del Reloj
etymology_summary: Named after the Casa del Reloj (Clock House), a prominent building on Avenida de Gibraltar 2 in central Leganes that houses municipal administrative services. The building features a distinctive clock tower that gives it its name. It serves as one of the main citizen service points of the Leganes city council.
named_after: Casa del Reloj (Arganzuela cultural centre, former clock-tower building)

name: Leganes Central
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the centre of Leganes. The municipality name most likely derives from 'legamo' or 'legano' (mud/silt), as recorded in the Relaciones Topograficas of Felipe II (1576), where town elders explained a lagoon with much silt existed at the town's founding site. Originally named 'Legamar' when founded in 1280 under Alfonso X, the name corrupted over time to Leganes.
source: Ayto. Leganes; Wikipedia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leganes; leganesactivo.com; secretosdeleganes.wordpress.com; toponhisp.org

name: San Nicasio
etymology_summary: Named after the San Nicasio neighbourhood in Leganes, which takes its name from the Ermita de San Nicasio (hermitage), built 1772-1780 by architect Ventura Rodriguez for the Marques de Leganes. San Nicasio (Saint Nicasius of Reims, d. 407) is the patron saint of Leganes. He was a Bishop of Reims martyred by Vandal invaders. Leganes adopted him as patron to seek protection from the plague epidemics that devastated the town, at the petition of Archbishop Cisneros to Pope Alexander VI.
source: Ayto. Leganes; Wikipedia; elartedelahistoria.wordpress.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicasius_of_Rheims; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Nicasio_(Leganes); leganesactivo.com
